newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Foreign investors wary of Nicaraguan elections.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors wary of Nicaraguan elections.

text.p: Nicaragua's increasingly polarized presidential elections are setting off alarm bells among foreign investors, business leaders said on Friday.

Most foreign investors would prefer a victory by conservative Arnoldo Aleman, but some fear his right-wing populist agenda will lead to clashes with the still-powerful Sandinistas and potential political instability.

"Investment will be reduced for a time following either a Sandinista victory or an Aleman victory, because both are extremes and there are fears as to how they will react after the election," Manuel Ignacio Lacayo, president of Coca Cola Nicaragua S.A., said in an interview.
As the October 20 vote approaches, the polls give Aleman a narrow lead over Sandinista candidate Daniel Ortega, who headed Nicaragua's Marxist government from 1979 to 1990.
The Sandinistas have shifted to the political center in 1996, promising to respect the laws of the free market if elected and work with private enterprise and foreign investors.

Investor doubts remain. They remember the 1980s when the Sandinistas confiscated private property and introduced a planned economy, and analysts said they would be initially wary of a Sandinista government.

Lacayo of Coca Cola said many businessmen were disappointed a centrist, conciliation candidate did not emerge as a credible third option to the Sandinistas and Aleman's virulently anti-Sandinista Liberal Alliance.

Carlos Pellas, head of Nicaragua's richest family, recently told a local television station foreign investors would hold back on investing in Nicaragua for the first two years of a Sandinista government to watch their attitude to business take shape.

This political uncertainty was felt on Thursday when officials canceled the planned partial sale of Nicaragua's state-run telephone company Empresa Nicaraguense de Telecomunicaciones (Enitel) until March 31, 1997.

The head of the Enitel privatization committee, Finance Minister Emilio Pereira, said investors had asked for the sale to be postponed until after the elections because of uncertainty surrounding the vote's results.

Other analysts said fears of a Sandinista victory and a return of socialism were exaggerated because whatever party wins they will have little economic room to maneuver given the agreements Nicaragua has signed with international lending institutions.

"Whoever wins the election, the attitude to investment in Nicaragua is not going to vary in a significant fashion," said Alejandro Martinez Cuenca, president of the International Foundation for the Global Economic Challenge.

"The circumstances facing the country at the end of the century will oblige the next government to continue the trend towards structural adjustment, deficit reduction and a smaller role for the state," Martinez Cuenca said.
